question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Green light
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. To permit something to proceed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Green light" means to give approval or permission for something to proceed or go ahead, just as a green traffic signal allows vehicles to move. (आगे बढ़ने की अनुमति देना)
◦ Example: The manager finally gave the green light for the new marketing campaign to begin.

• The expression comes from traffic signals, where green universally signals "go" and red signals "stop"; the idiom borrows this sense to mean official authorization.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To misunderstand — this means to fail to interpret something correctly; it has no connection with permission or approval.

• Option 3: To always compare — this is not an established idiomatic meaning of "green light" and does not relate to giving permission.

• Option 4: To be lost and confused — this describes bewilderment, which is unrelated to the idea of authorization conveyed by "green light".

NOTE

• Other colour-based idioms common in SSC exams: "To catch someone red-handed" (to catch in the act of wrongdoing), "Once in a blue moon" (very rarely), "To see red" (to become very angry), and "A white lie" (a harmless untruth).

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
He writes a paper every weekend.
option_1: A paper was written by him every weekend.
option_2: A paper is written by him every weekend.
option_3: A paper was been written by him every weekend.
option_4: A paper is been written by him every weekend.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. A paper is written by him every weekend.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "He writes a paper every weekend" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "a paper" becomes the subject; the auxiliary used is "is"; the verb "writes" becomes the past participle "written"; and "he" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: A paper is written by him every weekend.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was written" is the passive of the Simple Past Tense, not the Simple Present Tense used in the given sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "was been written" is not a grammatically valid verb form at all — "was" and "been" cannot occur together in this way.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "is been written" is similarly an invalid, non-existent verb form; the correct present-tense passive auxiliary is simply "is", not "is been".

NOTE

• The passive voice is formed with the appropriate form of "to be" + past participle (V3) of the main verb; the tense of the passive sentence must always match the tense of the active sentence.

• Common tense-passive auxiliary pairs tested in SSC: Simple Present → is/am/are, Simple Past → was/were, Present Perfect → has/have been, Simple Future → will be.

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Restricted
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Copious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Restricted" means limited, confined, or kept within certain bounds. (सीमित)

• Its opposite is "Copious", which means abundant, plentiful, or existing in large quantities, i.e., not limited or held back in any way. (प्रचुर, बहुत अधिक)
◦ Example: She took copious notes during the long lecture, unrestricted by any word limit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Finite (सीमित) — means having limits or bounds; this is a synonym, not an antonym, of "restricted".

• Option 3: Capped (सीमा तय की गई) — means having an upper limit imposed; this too is close in meaning to "restricted", not opposite to it.

• Option 4: Circumscribed (परिबद्ध) — means confined within limits or restricted; it is a near-synonym of "restricted", not its opposite.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "restricted" often confused as antonyms in SSC papers: confined, curbed, constrained, limited.

• Genuine antonyms of "restricted" to remember: copious, unlimited, boundless, unrestrained, ample.

question:
Choose the word that means the same as the given word.
Jarred
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Altercated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "Jarred" (from the verb "to jar") means to be in conflict or disagreement with someone; to clash or wrangle. (झगड़ा करना, टकराना)

• "Altercated" means had a noisy or heated argument/dispute with someone, which matches this sense of "jarred" exactly. (तीखी बहस करना)
◦ Example: The two neighbours jarred over the boundary wall and altercated loudly in the street.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Macho (मर्दाना) — means showily manly or aggressively virile; unrelated to conflict or disagreement.

• Option 2: Assented (सहमत होना) — means to express agreement or approval, which is nearly opposite to the idea of clashing conveyed by "jarred".

• Option 4: Accorded (प्रदान करना) — means to grant or give, or to be in agreement/harmony; this too is opposite in sense to "jarred".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "jarred" (to clash/disagree) with its more common sense of "to jolt or have an unpleasant, jarring physical effect" — SSC vocabulary lists test both senses.

• Related words for conflict often asked: wrangle, squabble, bicker, spar, feud.

question:
Some parts of a few sentences have been jumbled up, and labelled A, B, C and D. Select the option that gives the correct sequence in which these parts can be rearranged to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence
Our twelve years in the forest were
A. Ram had lost, we would have to
B. ending. Now, according to the wager
C. discovered our whereabouts, we would have to endure another ten years in exile
D. spend a year in hiding.
If during this year Mohan
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. BADC.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Reading the parts in the order B – A – D – C along with the fixed opening and closing lines gives a complete, meaningful passage:
◦ "Our twelve years in the forest were ending. Now, according to the wager Ram had lost, we would have to spend a year in hiding. If during this year Mohan discovered our whereabouts, we would have to endure another ten years in exile."

• The passage forms two connected statements: the first states that the twelve-year exile is ending (B) and explains the condition of the wager Ram had lost (A), which requires spending a year in hiding (D); the second is a conditional clause built on the fixed line "If during this year Mohan", completed by C, warning of a further penalty if they were discovered.

• Rule for sentence rearrangement: identify the part that logically connects to the fixed opening phrase first (here, "ending" directly completes "were ___"), then trace the cause-effect/conditional chain part by part.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (ACBD) is incorrect because it opens with "Ram had lost, we would have to" directly after "were", which does not grammatically or logically follow from the fixed opening line.

• Option 3 (CDAB) is incorrect because it places C ("discovered our whereabouts...") right after "were", producing a meaningless, disconnected statement.

• Option 4 (BDCA) is incorrect because although it correctly starts with B, it places D ("spend a year in hiding") before the wager has even been explained by A, breaking the logical cause-effect sequence.

NOTE

• In para-jumble/sentence-rearrangement questions, always locate the part that grammatically completes the fixed starting phrase first, then check pronoun references, conjunctions ("Now", "If") and logical/chronological order to fix the rest of the sequence.

• Time-bound or conditional clauses introduced by words like "If", "Now", "Then" are strong clues to correct placement, since they signal a shift in the narrative.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. BENIDICTION.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling of the word is "BENEDICTION" — a blessing, especially a short spoken invocation of God's blessing at the end of a religious service.
◦ Example: The priest gave the benediction as the congregation bowed their heads.

• Spelling key: BENE + DICTION. The prefix "bene-" (meaning "well/good", as in benefit, benevolent) is followed by "-diction" (related to "saying", as in dictate). The given option wrongly spells the second syllable as "BENI-" instead of "BENE-".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "CROCKERY" is correctly spelt — it refers to plates, cups, and other dishes made of earthenware or china.

• Option 2: "MOCKERY" is correctly spelt — it means ridicule or contemptuous action/speech.

• Option 3: "RELIGIOUS" is correctly spelt — note the sequence "-gious", a commonly misspelt ending.

NOTE

• Words built with the prefix "bene-" (good/well): benefit, benevolent, benefactor, benign — all keep the "e" after "ben".

• Commonly confused spelling pairs in SSC: maintenance/maintainance, occurrence/occurance, definitely/definately, embarrass/embarass.

question:
Rearrange the parts of the sentence in correct order.
Corruption is
P. misuse and abuse of public office, either directly
Q. typified by dishonesty, exploitation or the
R. or indirectly, for personal gains or unjust enrichment
S. in negation of due process or established protocol
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. QPRS.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Reading the parts in the order Q – P – R – S after the fixed opening "Corruption is" produces a complete, meaningful sentence:
◦ "Corruption is typified by dishonesty, exploitation or the misuse and abuse of public office, either directly or indirectly, for personal gains or unjust enrichment in negation of due process or established protocol."

• Rule for rearrangement: the part that completes the linking verb "is" most naturally must come first — here, Q ("typified by...") directly follows "Corruption is", since "is typified by" is a standard collocation. Part P then lists what corruption is typified by ("the misuse and abuse of public office"); R continues P's thought with "either directly or indirectly"; and S closes the sentence explaining the nature of that misuse.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (PSRQ) is incorrect because starting with P ("misuse and abuse of public office, either directly") right after "Corruption is" is grammatically awkward and breaks the natural "is typified by" construction.

• Option 3 (RSPQ) is incorrect because it begins with R ("or indirectly..."), which cannot logically follow "Corruption is" since "or" requires a preceding "either" clause that has not yet been introduced.

• Option 4 (PQSR) is incorrect because it places Q ("typified by...") in the middle rather than immediately after "Corruption is", disrupting the sentence's logical flow.

NOTE

• In such rearrangement questions, look first for the part that grammatically completes the given fixed phrase (verb, preposition, or article), and then trace connecting words like "either...or", "and", and pronouns to fix the remaining order.

• The correlative conjunction "either...or" must always keep its two parts adjacent in sequence, as seen with P and R here.

question:
Select the most appropriate 'one word' for the expression given below.
One who cures eye disease.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Ophthalmologist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• An "Ophthalmologist" is a medical doctor who specialises in diagnosing and treating diseases and disorders of the eye. (नेत्र रोग विशेषज्ञ)
◦ Example: She visited an ophthalmologist for her worsening eyesight.

• The word is formed from the Greek root "ophthalmos" meaning "eye", combined with the suffix "-ologist" meaning "one who studies/practises".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Biologist (जीव विज्ञानी) — one who studies living organisms in general, not specifically eye diseases.

• Option 2: Phonologist (ध्वनि विज्ञानी) — one who studies the sound system of a language; entirely unrelated to medicine.

• Option 3: Prologist — not a standard English word; it does not correspond to any recognised profession.

NOTE

• Other medical one-word substitutions frequently asked in SSC: Cardiologist (heart), Dermatologist (skin), Neurologist (nervous system), Orthopaedist (bones/joints), Pediatrician (children), Dentist (teeth).

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below
BLASPHEMOUS
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. DISRESPECTFUL.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Blasphemous" means showing contempt or lack of reverence for God or sacred things; profanely irreverent. (ईश-निंदा करने वाला, अनादरपूर्ण)

• "Disrespectful" means showing a lack of respect or reverence, which closely matches the irreverent quality expressed by "blasphemous". (अनादरपूर्ण)
◦ Example: His blasphemous remarks about the deity were seen as deeply disrespectful by the devotees.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: AUTHENTIC (प्रामाणिक) — means genuine or trustworthy; opposite in spirit to something profane or false.

• Option 3: COSTLY (महंगा) — relates to high price or expense, entirely unconnected to irreverence.

• Option 4: REALITY (वास्तविकता) — means the state of things as they actually exist; unrelated to disrespect or irreverence.

NOTE

• Related words: profane, sacrilegious, irreverent, impious are all synonyms of "blasphemous"; their opposites are reverent, pious, devout.

question:
Select the option that will improve the (bracketed) part of the sentence. In case of no improvement select the option 'No improvement'.
The play was (either as funny or as) disturbing as Shivang told it was.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. neither as funny nor as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence compares two qualities of the play ("funny" and "disturbing") in a negative equal comparison, which requires the correlative conjunction pair "neither...nor", not "either...or".

• Rule — Correlative conjunctions: "either" must always be paired with "or", and "neither" must always be paired with "nor". They cannot be mixed.

• Applying the rule: "The play was neither as funny nor as disturbing as Shivang told it was" correctly conveys that the play was not as funny, and also not as disturbing, as described.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original bracketed phrase "either as funny or as" does not fit the negative sense the sentence requires with "neither/nor".

• Option 2: "either as funny nor as" is incorrect because it wrongly mixes "either" with "nor" — a mismatched correlative pair.

• Option 4: "neither as funny or as" is incorrect because it wrongly mixes "neither" with "or" instead of the required "nor".

NOTE

• Other commonly tested correlative conjunction pairs in SSC: not only...but also, both...and, whether...or, such...that.

• A frequent error type is mixing these fixed pairs (e.g., "either...nor", "neither...or") — always check that the two halves of a correlative pair match.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Fashion might not be first thing that comes to mind when we think of isolation strategies.
option_2: thing that comes to mind when
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Fashion might not be first.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The segment "Fashion might not be first" is missing the definite article "the" before the ordinal "first".

• Rule: When "first" (or any ordinal number used as an adjective before a noun, as in "the first thing") introduces a specific, unique item being singled out, it must be preceded by the definite article "the".

• Corrected sentence: "Fashion might not be the first thing that comes to mind when we think of isolation strategies."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because there is indeed a grammatical error in the sentence — the missing article discussed above.

• Option 2: "thing that comes to mind when" is correct as printed and contains no grammatical fault.

• Option 3: "we think of isolation strategies." is correct as printed and contains no grammatical fault.

NOTE

• Ordinal numbers/superlative-type expressions (first, best, only, main, most important) used to single out one item from a group almost always require the definite article "the" before them.

• Common SSC error-spotting trap: missing or wrongly used articles (a/an/the) before singular countable nouns and ordinal/superlative adjectives.

question:
Choose the option that is the correct indirect form of the sentence.
She said to her, "Please pay attention to the details."
option_1: She requests her that pay attention to the details.
option_2: She commanded her for paying attention to the details.
option_3: She requested her to pay attention to the details.
option_4: She requested her that to pay attention to the details.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. She requested her to pay attention to the details.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The direct speech "Please pay attention to the details" is an imperative sentence expressing a polite request (signalled by the word "Please").

• Rule — Reporting a request (imperative sentence with "Please"): the reporting verb "said" changes to "requested", the word "Please" is dropped, and the imperative verb is converted to the infinitive ("to" + base verb). The structure is: Subject + requested + Object + to + V1 + rest of sentence.

• Applying the rule: "She said to her, 'Please pay attention to the details'" becomes "She requested her to pay attention to the details."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "requests" wrongly keeps the present tense (it should be "requested" to match the reporting verb "said"), and "that pay attention" is not a grammatically valid construction for reporting a request.

• Option 2 is incorrect because "commanded" changes the tone from a polite request to an order, which does not match the word "Please" in the original sentence; requests should use "requested", not "commanded".

• Option 4 is incorrect because it wrongly combines "that" with the infinitive "to pay" — a request reported with "requested" must use only the infinitive form, never "that" together with "to".

NOTE

• Imperative sentences with "Please" → reported using "requested"; imperative sentences that are orders (without "please") → reported using "ordered/commanded"; imperative sentences with "Let us" → reported using "suggested".

• The reported imperative always takes the infinitive (to + V1) form, never a "that" clause.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
A fully grow Chihuahua weighs less than the average house cat.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. fully grown.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The underlined phrase "fully grow" uses the base form "grow" as an adjective before the noun "Chihuahua", which is grammatically incorrect.

• Rule: To describe a noun as having reached its complete/mature state, the past participle (V3) "grown" must be used as an adjective, not the base verb form. "Fully" is an adverb correctly modifying the participial adjective "grown".

• Corrected sentence: "A fully grown Chihuahua weighs less than the average house cat."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No improvement" is incorrect because the base form "grow" cannot function as an adjective before a noun; an error is clearly present.

• Option 3: "fullest grown" is incorrect because "full" is not gradable in this adjectival sense, and the superlative form "fullest" cannot combine with "grown" in standard usage.

• Option 4: "fully growth" is incorrect because "growth" is a noun, not a participial adjective, and cannot be used to modify "Chihuahua" in this position.

NOTE

• Common V1–V3 adjective confusions tested in SSC: grow/grown, break/broken, write/written, speak/spoken, choose/chosen — the past participle (V3) form is used adjectivally, not the base form (V1).

• Adverbs like "fully", "fully-fledged", "well" commonly precede participial adjectives (e.g., "fully grown", "well written", "fully equipped").

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
It is important to ensure that we all have good clean water to drink that is not ________ by heavy metals or chemicals.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. contaminated.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence talks about water being made impure or unsafe "by heavy metals or chemicals" — the verb that correctly collocates with this idea is "contaminated", meaning to make impure or poisonous by exposure to or addition of a harmful substance.

• Rule — Contextual word choice: the chosen word must logically pair with the agent introduced by "by" (here, "heavy metals or chemicals"); only "contaminated" naturally follows "not ________ by [a harmful substance]".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "purged" means cleansed or rid of something unwanted; it is nearly opposite to what is meant here, and does not logically combine with "by heavy metals" in the negative sense the sentence requires.

• Option 3: "clarified" means made clear or pure (often used for liquids like butter); it does not fit the sense of harmful contamination "by heavy metals or chemicals".

• Option 4: "knotted" means tied into a knot or tangled; it is entirely unrelated to water quality or pollution.

NOTE

• Words related to pollution/impurity frequently tested together: contaminate, pollute, adulterate, taint, corrupt (in the sense of making impure).

• Their opposites: purify, cleanse, refine, decontaminate.

question:
Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
They know they will face / either a swift backlash / or deafening silence.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. No error.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "They know they will face either a swift backlash or deafening silence" is grammatically correct in every part.

• Rule — Correlative conjunction "either...or": the two elements joined by "either" and "or" must be grammatically parallel. Here, "a swift backlash" and "deafening silence" are both noun phrases, so the parallelism is correctly maintained.

• The subject-verb agreement ("They know"), the future tense ("will face"), and the correlative pairing ("either...or") are all used correctly, so no part of the sentence contains an error.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "or deafening silence." is grammatically correct; it is a properly parallel noun phrase matching "a swift backlash".

• Option 3: "They know they will face" is grammatically correct; subject-verb agreement and tense are both proper.

• Option 4: "either a swift backlash" is grammatically correct; it correctly introduces the first half of the "either...or" pair.

NOTE

• In "No error"-type questions, always check subject-verb agreement, tense consistency, article usage, and parallel structure in correlative conjunctions (either/or, neither/nor, not only/but also) before concluding there is an error.

• Do not force-find an error where standard grammar rules are correctly followed — "No error" is the correct choice whenever the sentence is fully grammatical.

question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. SABOTAGE.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "SABOTAGE" is the correctly spelt word, meaning the deliberate destruction, disruption, or damage of something, especially for political or military advantage.
◦ Example: The factory fire was later found to be an act of sabotage.

• Spelling key: SABO + TAGE. The word comes from French, and ends in the distinctive "-tage".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "PRECISSION" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "PRECISION" — a single "S", not double.

• Option 2: "MISSIONERY" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "MISSIONARY" — the ending is "-ary", not "-ery".

• Option 4: "MEALIGN" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "MALIGN" — there is no "E" after the "M".

NOTE

• Common single/double-letter spelling traps in SSC: PRECISION (not precission), NECESSARY (one C, two S), OCCASION (two C, one S), EMBARRASS (two R, two S).

• Words ending in "-ary" vs "-ery": MISSIONARY, DICTIONARY, STATIONARY (adjective, meaning not moving) are commonly confused with STATIONERY (noun, meaning paper/pens).

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
All and sundry
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Everyone without distinction.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "All and sundry" means everybody, without exception or distinction; every kind of person, important or not. (हर कोई, बिना किसी भेदभाव के)
◦ Example: The free food stall was open to all and sundry at the fair.

• The phrase pairs "all" (everyone) with the archaic word "sundry" (various, miscellaneous individuals), together emphasising inclusiveness of every single person.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Full moon — refers to the lunar phase when the moon is fully illuminated; unrelated to the idiom's meaning.

• Option 2: Advantages and disadvantages — refers to pros and cons of a matter, which has no connection with the idea of "everyone" expressed by the idiom.

• Option 3: Holidays — refers to days of rest or vacation, entirely unrelated to the idiom's meaning.

NOTE

• The word "sundry" also appears in the common phrase "sundry items", meaning miscellaneous or various small items.

• Other idioms of universality tested in SSC: "Every Tom, Dick and Harry" (any ordinary person), "Rank and file" (ordinary members of a group).

question:
Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank.
This has given rise to the view that the legal code is __________ against women and the poor.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. biased.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence discusses a view that the legal code unfairly favours one side over another — "biased" means showing an unfair preference or prejudice for or against someone/something, which correctly fits the context "biased against women and the poor".

• Rule — Contextual word choice: the word must collocate naturally with "against"; the standard collocation "biased against" is a common, fixed usage, unlike the other options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "baked" means cooked by dry heat, or (informally) set/finalised; it makes no sense in the context of a legal code being unfair.

• Option 2: "frank" means open and honest in expression; it does not logically combine with "against" to describe unfairness in a legal code.

• Option 3: "duplicitous" means deceitful or double-dealing; while negative, it describes dishonesty rather than one-sided unfairness, and does not collocate naturally with "against" in this sense.

NOTE

• Common collocations with "biased": biased against, biased in favour of, biased towards.

• Related words for unfairness often tested: prejudiced, partial, discriminatory, one-sided — their opposites are impartial, unbiased, neutral, even-handed.

question:
Select the word that is similar in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below
Efficacy
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Efficiency.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Efficacy" means the ability to produce a desired or intended result; effectiveness. (प्रभावशीलता, सक्षमता)

• "Efficiency" means the ability to achieve a result with the least waste of time and effort; effectiveness in producing results, which closely matches the sense of "efficacy". (कार्यकुशलता)
◦ Example: Doctors confirmed the efficacy of the new vaccine after successful trials, praising its efficiency in preventing infection.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Futility (व्यर्थता) — means uselessness or pointlessness; this is nearly opposite in meaning to "efficacy".

• Option 3: Impotence (अक्षमता) — means lack of power or ability to produce an effect; this is essentially the antonym of "efficacy".

• Option 4: Ineptness (अक्षमता, अयोग्यता) — means lack of skill or competence; this too is opposite in sense to "efficacy".

NOTE

• Do not confuse "efficacy" (ability to produce a desired effect, used especially for medicines/treatments/policies) with "efficiency" (achieving a result without wasting resources) — though closely related, they are typically tested as near-synonyms in SSC vocabulary sets.

• Antonyms of "efficacy" to remember: inefficacy, futility, ineffectiveness, impotence.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
A person who is never happy with what he has
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Malcontent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• A "Malcontent" is a person who is chronically dissatisfied or discontented, never happy or satisfied with their circumstances. (असंतुष्ट व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: The malcontent employee complained about every new policy, however beneficial.

• The word is formed from the prefix "mal-" (bad/ill, as in malfunction, malpractice) and "content" (satisfied) — literally, one who is "badly/not content".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Miser (कंजूस) — a person who hoards money and is unwilling to spend it; describes stinginess, not general dissatisfaction.

• Option 2: Heresy (विधर्म) — this is an abstract noun meaning a belief contrary to accepted religious doctrine; it does not describe a person at all.

• Option 4: Malleable (लचीला, ढलनशील) — describes something (metal or a person's character) that can be easily shaped or influenced; unrelated to perpetual dissatisfaction.

NOTE

• Other "mal-" prefixed words common in SSC one-word substitutions: malevolent (wishing harm to others), malnourished (poorly fed), malefactor (a wrongdoer).

• Contrast with "content/contented" (satisfied) and "optimist" (a generally hopeful, positive person) — opposite personality types to "malcontent".

There were other stories (1) ________ Krishna. How (2) ________ been born in a dungeon where his uncle Kamsa had imprisoned his parents with the intention of killing him at birth. Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. about.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank requires a preposition that correctly follows the phrase "stories ___ Krishna"; the standard, natural collocation is "stories about someone", meaning narratives concerning or describing that person.

• Rule: The preposition "about" is used after nouns like "story", "talk", "book", "information" etc. to indicate the subject matter being discussed.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "belonging to" would indicate possession/ownership of the stories by Krishna, not that the stories are concerning him; it does not fit the intended meaning.

• Option 2: "with respect" is grammatically incomplete here — the full standard phrase would need to be "with respect to", and even then it sounds unnatural before a proper noun like "Krishna" in this context.

• Option 3: "upon" does not collocate naturally with "stories" in the sense of narrating tales concerning a person.

NOTE

• Common preposition-noun collocations tested in SSC cloze passages: stories/talk/news about someone, information/knowledge about something, fond of, interested in, good at.

• Always read the full sentence context to identify the exact collocation expected, rather than translating literally.

How he lifted up Mount Govardhan to shelter his people from a (5) ________ that would have drowned them.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. he had.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The passage narrates past events about Krishna's birth using "How ___ been born in a dungeon...", which requires the Past Perfect Tense (had + V3) to describe an action completed before another past point in the narrative.

• Rule — Past Perfect Tense: Subject + had + V3 (past participle). Here, the sentence needs "he had been born" to match the tense of the surrounding narrative, which uses "had been imprisoned", "had been spirited" etc.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "he has" is incorrect because "has been born" is Present Perfect Tense, which does not match the past narrative tense used throughout the passage.

• Option 3: "he have" is incorrect because it is grammatically wrong — "have" does not agree with the third-person singular subject "he" (it should be "has"), and even so, it would still be the wrong tense.

• Option 4: "he was" is incorrect because "was been born" is not a valid English verb construction — "was" and "been" cannot combine directly in this way.

NOTE

• The whole passage consistently uses the Past Perfect Tense ("had imprisoned", "had been spirited") to narrate events that happened before the main past narrative point, so all blanks referring to earlier completed actions should match this tense.

• Common tense-consistency errors in cloze passages: mixing present perfect/simple past with past perfect within a single continuous narrative.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. away.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank completes the phrasal verb "spirited away", which means carried off secretly and swiftly, especially so as to avoid detection or capture.

• Rule — Phrasal verb collocation: "spirit" used as a verb almost always combines with the particle "away" to form the fixed phrasal verb "spirit away"; no other particle produces this meaning.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "together" does not form any recognised phrasal verb with "spirited" and does not fit the context of secretly removing the infant to safety.

• Option 2: "gone" is grammatically incorrect here, since it does not combine with "spirited" to form a valid phrase.

• Option 4: "around" does not form a meaningful phrasal verb with "spirited" in this context of secret escape.

NOTE

• Other common phrasal verbs with fixed particles tested in SSC: carried away, whisked away, taken away, run away, give away.

• "Spirit away" specifically connotes a mysterious or magical removal, fitting the miraculous tone of the passage describing Krishna's escape from the dungeon.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. demoness.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is followed by "who tried to poison him with her breast milk" — the pronoun "her" clearly indicates that the person being described is female, so the noun filling the blank must also be female.

• Rule — Gender agreement: the noun used to describe a person must agree in gender with the pronouns referring back to that person later in the sentence. Since "her" is used, the correct word is the feminine "demoness", referring to the mythological figure Putana who tried to poison the infant Krishna with poisoned breast milk.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "satan" refers to the devil, a masculine figure in Judeo-Christian tradition; it does not agree with the feminine pronoun "her" and is contextually unrelated to this Krishna legend.

• Option 2: "god" is a masculine noun and does not agree with the feminine pronoun "her" used later in the sentence.

• Option 3: "demon" is typically used as a masculine or gender-neutral noun in English and does not specifically agree with the feminine "her"; the passage requires the explicitly feminine form.

NOTE

• Gender-specific noun pairs commonly tested in SSC: demon/demoness, host/hostess, actor/actress, hero/heroine, prince/princess.

• Pronoun agreement (he/she/his/her) later in a sentence is a reliable clue for selecting the correctly gendered noun in a cloze blank.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. deluge.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is followed by "that would have drowned them", indicating a large-scale flood of water — "deluge" means a severe flood; a great and destructive downpour or flood of water, which precisely fits the context.

• Rule — Contextual word choice: the correct word must specifically denote a flood or flood-causing event capable of "drowning" people, since "drowned" collocates specifically with water-related disasters.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "earthquake" refers to a sudden violent shaking of the ground; while destructive, an earthquake does not "drown" people, so it does not logically fit with "would have drowned them".

• Option 2: "drought" refers to a prolonged shortage of water/rainfall — the opposite of a flood — and cannot logically cause drowning.

• Option 4: "snowfall" refers to falling snow; while heavy snow can cause other hazards, it is not typically described as something that would "drown" people the way a flood does.

NOTE

• This refers to the well-known legend of Krishna lifting Mount Govardhan to shelter the people of Gokul from the torrential rains/flood sent by the deity Indra.

• Context clues involving specific consequence verbs (here, "drowned") are key to selecting the correct word among superficially similar disaster-related options in cloze passages.
